item.title: Website Templates
item.dc:creator: tsieb
item.content:encoded:
• Course Templates
  • Portfolio Templates
  • Assignment Templates
  • Research & Professional Templates
  • SPLOT Templates

Need a template customized?

All website themes are customizable and can be adapted to suit specific contexts and situations. Customizing a template can include updating the images, the menu links, and writing prompts to reflect your project’s completion criteria.

Connect with the LT&I team at learningtech@tru.ca to discuss your project so we can collaboratively customize a template for you and visit your classroom to support student website development.

Course Templates

Displaying course information on a website makes the information open and accessible and provides opportunities for creativity. The level of student interaction is up to you!

Portfolio Templates

Website portfolios provide students with a space to curate and showcase their learning while developing their digital literacy skills. Students can control the privacy of the site through site settings and password protected pages.

Assignment Templates

A great companion to some authentic and meaningful assessments are websites. They can be designed for students to complete work individually, collaboratively in small groups, or collaboratively class-wide.

Research & Professional Templates

Building a website for research and professional initiatives creates an open access space for documenting and presenting processes, findings, and professional works.

SPLOT Templates

SPLOT templates help you create simple, collaborative WordPress sites for your teaching. They are designed with two core principles in mind:

  • make it as easy as possible to post activity to the open web in an appealing and accessible way and
  • allow users to do so without creating accounts, or providing any required personal information.

item.title: Using Gradebook in Moodle
item.dc:creator: troy
item.content:encoded: In this workshop, you work in a small group to set up a gradebook, including adding categories, grade items and assignment weighting. Registration is limited to three participants per session.
item.excerpt:encoded: A hands-on session focusing on Moodle's assessment and grade reporting tools.

item.title: Bringing Content to Life with H5P
item.dc:creator: troy
item.content:encoded: Add engaging, interactive learning activities to your Moodle course or WordPress site using H5P— a user-friendly web authoring tool that requires little technical knowledge or proficiency. Create activities and learning objects that will help your students succeed in your class, and possibly have fun while doing so. Activities commonly created with H5P include: annotated visuals (i.e., hotspots); interactive videos; and branching scenarios. In this interactive session participants will have the opportunity to create these kinds of activities in Moodle or WordPress.
item.excerpt:encoded: Learn how to add engaging, interactive learning activities to your Moodle course or WordPress site using H5P. You'll be building multimedia in minutes.

item.title: Orientation to Moodle
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: In this workshop, faculty learn how to set up a basic Moodle course shell, practise letting students join using a registration code, and make use of the editing, document uploading, and privacy functions. Registration in each workshop is limited to six participants.
item.excerpt:encoded: A beginner-level introduction to Moodle, TRU's learning management system, and an overview of the essential steps.

item.title: Using Big Blue Button
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: Did you know you can allow others to connect remotely to your course through Moodle? Big Blue Button lets you create links to real-time online classrooms. This open source web conferencing system can be used for distance learning, to allow groups to connect remotely, or to bring in guest speakers. You can also use it to save and view recordings. Registration in this workshop is limited to six participants.
item.excerpt:encoded: BBB connects with Moodle to allow for remote classroom and videoconferencing applications.

item.title: Creating Interactive Content Using H5P
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: Did you know you can create interactive content in Moodle using H5P? This open source software allows you to create rich and interactive web experiences more efficiently. With H5P, you may create and edit interactive videos, presentations, games, timelines and more. In addition to being an authoring tool for rich content, H5P enables you to import and export H5P files for effective reuse and sharing of content. Registration in this workshop is limited to six participants.
item.excerpt:encoded: H5P allows everyone to create rich and interactive web experiences, and it is integrated with TRU's Moodle.

item.title: Using Scheduler
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: Did you know you can specify time slots and allow students to schedule meetings with you? You can record the outcome of the meeting, the note can be made visible to students or kept confidential (visible to you only). Group scheduling is supported; that is, each time slot can accommodate several students, and optionally it is possible to schedule appointments for entire groups at the same time. Registration in this workshop is limited to six participants.
item.excerpt:encoded: Moodle's Scheduler function allows you to define time slots or office hours and allow students to schedule meetings with you.

item.title: Using Video in Moodle
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded:
Kaltura is a place where students and faculty can create, upload, manage, publish, deliver quality video and share it with others. You can think of it as a TRU's version of YouTube. This service is offered to the TRU community at no cost.

Kaltura works with Moodle, we have implemented the integration of Moodle and Kaltura. Students will be able to create and submit video assignments, contribute to course media galleries as well as receive audio or video feedback. Like Moodle Kaltura is mobile friendly.
item.excerpt:encoded: Moodle supports webcam video posting and commenting. TRU is also launching Kaltura, a powerful online video platform which integrates with Moodle.

item.title: Curating the Web with Wikimedia and the Kumu Wiki
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: Wikipedia is “the largest and most popular general reference work on the World Wide Web” (Wikipedia, 2018).  TRU hosts its own Wiki system— Kumu Wiki— which can be used by TRU faculty, staff, and students for knowledge creation and sharing. In this interactive workshop participants will have the opportunity to register as Kumu Wiki users, and create a wiki on a topic of interest. We will also discuss and explore how Kumu Wiki can be used in your class to help students engage in public, authentic, meaningful learning activities including writing, editing, and publishing.
item.excerpt:encoded: Explore how Wikipedia and the Wikimedia Commons can provide a wealth of open resources and powerful learning activities. Get acquainted with TRU's own instance of MediaWiki -- Kumu.

item.title: Building Your Learning Technology Toolkit
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: Preparing to teach using educational technology can be, for some, challenging or overwhelming. At TRU, we can support you as you use Moodle, WordPress, or other technologies to expand or enhance your teaching practice. For those who are just starting out using technology, or for more experienced users, a “toolkit” or “sandbox site” in Moodle or WordPress can give you a place to experiment, as well as develop resources or learning activities before sharing them with students. In this interactive session participants will have the opportunity to create a multi-purpose learning technology “sandbox” or “toolkit” in Moodle or WordPress.
item.excerpt:encoded: A “toolkit” or “sandbox site” in Moodle or WordPress can give you a place to experiment, as well as develop resources or learning activities before sharing them with students.

item.title: LMS, Open Web, or Both?
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: TRU offers faculty, staff, and students support using Moodle as a learning management software (LMS) platform. But there are other options as well. We also host, on campus-based servers, learning technologies which exist on the open web— that is, websites and other applications which do not require signing in through TRU’s institutional website— such as WordPress publishing, Mattermost chatting, Kumu Wiki for knowledge building and sharing, and others. In this discussion-focused workshop we will explore the affordances, constraints, capabilities, and areas of overlap between and among learning management software applications (LMS) such as Moodle, and applications which exist on the open web— such as WordPress. Examples of TRU faculty, staff, and student WordPress sites will be shared. Participants will have the opportunity to register for WordPress, Mattermost, or other types of accounts, and find out more about the options for support and professional development using these technologies.
item.excerpt:encoded: In this discussion-focused workshop we will explore the affordances, constraints, capabilities, and areas of overlap between and among learning management software applications (LMS) such as Moodle, and applications which exist on the open web— such as WordPress.

item.title: Student Privacy and the Open Web
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: There is a wide range of websites and online applications which have the potential to enhance student engagement and success. Instructors have used Google applications such as Docs and Slides, video hosting sites such as YouTube or Vimeo, survey and audience response sites, as well as many others. Many of these applications collect user data and store these on servers located outside Canada, and can potentially use this data in ways that compromise students’ rights to privacy and their ownership over their data. In this discussion-based workshop, we will explore points to consider when creating assignments and projects using these platforms, and how TRU-hosted educational technology options including WordPress (websites and publishing); Mattermost (chats, discussions, and team-building); Kumu Wiki (knowledge-building and sharing); and others can help ensure your assignments and projects are engaging and respectful of students’ rights to privacy.
item.excerpt:encoded: We will review the legal and ethical dimensions of online data collection. This will cover both TRU-hosted applications as well as external tools.

item.title: Course Templates
item.dc:creator: joebinns
item.content:encoded:
Simple Course Template

Based on the OpenEd Canvas Clone theme, this template features a left side menu, customizable sections and navigational buttons. This template works well for large or small course when you want to keep the visual aesthetics simple and clean. 

Beyond Moodle Course Template

Based on the McLuhan theme, this template features a left side menu, imagery and multi page design. This template works well for large or small text heavy course.

Single Page Course Template

Based on the Kadence theme, this template features a unique layout, engaging visuals, and customizable sections. This template works well for small courses where only one page is needed.

item.title: Porfolio Templates
item.dc:creator: joebinns
item.content:encoded:
Public Relations ePortfolio Template

Based on the McLuhan theme, this template features a left-hand menu, customizable pages and sections. This template works well for large or small text heavy projects.

TESL Portfolio Template

Based on the Rams theme, featuring a professional layout and left-hand menu, this template allows you to create an impressive portfolio with multiple pages to showcase your work. This template is easy for students to use and can be adapted to any smaller multi-part project.

Adventure Studies ePortfolio Template

Based on the Hoffman theme, this template features a collapsed menu with customizable menu items and social media icons. This template works well with large or small multi-part projects and can be customized to suit your needs.

Visual Arts ePortfolio Template

Based on the Fukasawa theme, this template features a left hand menu with customizable sections. The “works” page features a series of images that link to individual posts. The Fukasawa theme is one of the more technical themes to work with but is also one of the more visually pleasing themes. This template can be adapted to any large or small project.

Visual Arts Grid Template

Based on the Hamilton theme, this template is highly visual featuring a series of images on the main page, in a visual block format, that link to individual posts. This template is easy to use and works well with small or large projects, the order the images display is determined by the posts timestamps so if you change the timestamp you change the order.

Portfolio Grid Template

Based on the Ascend theme, this template features a drop down menu, customizable pages and uses a responsive grid layout to organize content. This template is highly customizable but does look best with an even number of pages so the grid remains intact. It is suitable for large or small projects but is not suitable for the first time website builder.

Microcredential Capstone Template - Environmental Sustainability

Based on the Cover theme, this template features a pop out menu, customizable sections, and visually engaging page elements. This template can be adapted for any large or small multi-part project. 

Microcredential Capstone Template - Global Leadership

Based on the Cover theme, features a customizable top menu,, visually engaging page, and clickable images leading to individual posts for showcasing projects or portfolio. This template can be adapted for any large or small multi-part project. 

Essential Skills Training ePortfolio Template

Based on the Lovecraft theme, this template offers a sleek design with a top menu and customizable pages for seamless content organization and navigation.

Education ePortfolio Template

Based on Twenty Seventeen theme, this template provides a user-friendly interface for organizing course materials and resources efficiently along with engaging imagery. This template is easy to use and can be adapted for any large or small project.

item.title: SPLOT Templates
item.dc:creator: joebinns
item.content:encoded:
ITC Global Template

Based on the TRU writer theme, this template allows people to submit text-based content which creates a post and displays in a gallery for others to browse.

SPLOT Point Master Template

Based on the Splotbox theme, features images, navigational bar, search bar and file submission form.

SPLOT Box Master Template

Based on SPLOTpoint theme, this template includes a collapsible navigation bar, navigational buttons and customizable sections.

SPLOT Writer Master Template

Based on the Site Health screen theme, this is a mostly blank template featuring a top navigation bar, search bar and submission form.

SPLOT Collector Master Template

Based on the TRU Collector theme, this template includes a left-side navigation bar, file submission form and search bar.

Toolset Submitter

Based on the Kadence theme, this site allows people to submit a variety of file types (e.g. image, text, file, audio, etc.) which creates a post and displays in a gallery for others to browse.

item.title: Assignment Templates
item.dc:creator: joebinns
item.content:encoded:
Family Resources Template

Based on the Baskerville theme, this theme gives you a starting point with a top navigation bar, imagery and multi page design. This template can be easily customized for any multi-page assignment. It can also be used as a space to hold multiple assignments. 

Video Template

Based on the Pinnacle Child Video Project theme, it features a menu at the top and a submission page. This template is for a group video project and can be customized by you, you can pick a new banner image and the project's title and description will be updated accordingly. Originally students were to create a poster and a video, the poster is uploaded in the featured image section of the submission form. The featured image could be any image that students select based on the assignments criteria. Take a look at a finished project site https://implicit-bias-project-section1.trubox.ca/ 

Gamification Template

Based on the Twenty Seventeen theme, it features customizable sections, imagery and H5P elements. This template is perfect for assessments that require students to build an H5P activity.

item.title: Research and Professional Templates
item.dc:creator: joebinns
item.content:encoded:
Podcast Site Template

Based on the Twenty Twelve theme, this template is perfect for creating podcasts, it includes a top navigation bar, imagery, multi-page design and podcasting resources.

Single Page ePortfolio Template

Based on the Garfunkel theme, this template features a drop down menu, engaging and professional visuals, interactive page elements, and customizable sections. This template works best for projects that require all information to be displayed on one page.

Multiple Page ePortfolio Template

Based on the Kadence theme, this template features a pop out navigation menu, multi-page design with subpages, and background imagery. This template can be easily customized for any multi-page assignment. It can also be used as a space to hold multiple assignments. 

Sample Tenure Portfolio

Based on the Twenty Fifteen theme, this template includes TRU-branding, pop out navigation menu, multi-page design and subpages. This template works well for large or small text heavy projects.

TRU Branding Template

Based on the Kadence theme, this template features TRU-branding and can be used to present your research or professional information. This template can be easily customized for any multi-page assignment. It can also be used as a space to hold multiple assignments.

item.title: New Faculty Orientation
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded:
We are Learning Technology & Innovation (LT&I)

LT&I complement CELT, and TRU IT, supporting teaching and learning. Our Production and Media teams build online and distance courses for Open Learning, while the Learning Technology team is focused on supporting TRU's learners, teachers, and campus community. Our site: https://lti.trubox.ca

Office Hours

Drop in to our virtual office hours every Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday to have your learning technology questions answered.

The Learning Management system

Access: https://moodle.tru.ca – Login using your TRU ID. Course “shells”, instructor assignment and student enrolments mirror the Course Schedule

Moodle Orientation is our best and most concise resource for help documentation, tutorials and FAQs. https://moodleorientation.trubox.ca.

Teaching and meeting online

‘BBB’ is integrated into Moodle, but you can access it for your private use as well.

https://bigblue1.tru.ca

BigBlueButton is integrated into Moodle for virtual office hours, meetings and online classes. Recordings are automatically archived into your Moodle course, (although you are not able to edit them directly).

Zoom accounts are also available to all TRU users: https://tru-ca.zoom.us/

Upload and share your videos

Students can watch your videos in Moodle or you can share to a wider audience.

https://media.tru.ca

Kaltura is used for hosting videos, and is fully integrated into Moodle as well. Create and embed videos into your Moodle course, or have students submit video assignments. Kaltura Recorder is available to make simple screencasts but get in touch if you need to do a more complex presentation.

Publish online courses, e-portfolios, research

We maintain an instance of WordPress at https://trubox.ca and are founding partners of the BC OpenETC.

Some samples of what WordPress can do are on this LT&I Showcase site.

The TRU Open Press

"empowers students and educators to create educational
resources with professional support and financial opportunities."

https://openpress.trubox.ca

Artificial Intelligence and Education

Are you concerned and confused about the impacts of AI on our practice as educators? So are we! We've been developing an iterative resource with resources, classroom ideas, and suggested language for a syllabus: https://aieducation.trubox.ca/

Our LT&I site has starter resources on accessibility, multimedia design, video creation, alternative assessments and more.

LT&I also offer a suit of workshops each semester that are not just on Moodle, while we offer those to, we like to include a range of online learning tools and strategies. Join us to learn more about what Moodle can do for you, get a creative spark to learn and try something new or gain a little professional development. Check out our offerings at https://lti.trubox.ca/workshops-courses/. Browse the opportunities and let us know if there is something you are interested in learning more about that isn't offered!

Of special interest is the Inclusive Digital Design Course, this program gives faculty and staff the opportunity to learn how to make learning materials more inclusive and learner-centered. The self-study materials are on Open Courses (TRU's version of Open Moodle), and we will be offering a supported cohort again later this year.

Supported tools can be viewed at: https://lti.trubox.ca/browse-tools/

Communicating with students and/or amongst teams can be hard. LT&I offers Mattermost as an alternative online communication system, an open source system similar to Slack: https://matter.tru.ca. Contact us for more information regarding Mattermost.

Meet the TRU community

While on hiatus this year, You Got This! for a wonderful series of conversations with a broad and diverse representation of TRU's learning and teaching community. https://yougotthis.trubox.ca/

Contact us:

Director of LT&I: Brian Lamb blamb@tru.ca

Support team:
Coordinators, Educational Technologies: Jamie Drozda, Melanie Latham, Brad Forsyth, Brenna Clarke Gray (on leave)
Learning Technologists: 

Email:
moodlesupport@tru.ca and/or learningtech@tru.ca

item.title: LT&I Showcase
item.dc:creator: bforsyth
item.content:encoded:
We are Learning Technology & Innovation (LT&I)

LT&I’s mission is to provide learner-centered, sustainable technology tools and support for TRU’s diverse community. We are dedicated to enhancing the quality and flexibility of education, research, and scholarship through effective, inclusive, and ethical technological practices.

LT&I complement CELT, and TRU IT. Our Production and Media teams build online and distance courses for Open Learning, while the Learning Technology team is focused on supporting TRU's learners, teachers, and campus community.

The Learning Management system

The LT&I team supports the TRU community (faculty, OLFMs, and students) with Moodle through several channels.

Moodle Orientation is our best and most concise resource for help documentation, tutorials and FAQs. 

Other Learning Technologies We Support

In addition to Moodle, The LT&I team supports the TRU community with a variety of other learning technologies through our ticketing system, virtual office hours, consultations, and programming.

  • WordPress
  • PressBooks
  • BigBlueButton
  • Kaltura
  • H5P
  • Lightboard
  • Mattermost
  • Slido

Our LT&I site also has starter resources on accessibility, multimedia design, video creation, alternative assessments and more.

Promoting Inclusive & Accessible Practices

Through the development of internal resources and programming, as well as through collaboration with campus partners, the LT&I team strives to promote inclusive and accessible practices through a proactive rather than a reactive approach.

Inclusive Digital Design / Inclusive Poster Design / Poster Submission Template
Moodle Course Design - What's Possible?

Artificial Intelligence in Education (Including Guidance) / Let's try AI (student activities) (Digital Detox / GenAI Quickstart

Responding to Generative AI

While we expect developments in artificial intelligence to continue to rapidly change, the Learning Technology and Innovation team and other campus partners are working together to stay on top of developments and share emerging best practices with our community. We do this by continuously revising support resources, developing learning opportunities, providing specialized workshops for faculties, and through the planned AI Collaboratory space.

Promoting Open Educational Practices

LT&I is recognized as a leader in open educational technologies, enabling us to extend our reach through open educational resources and open pedagogy. Our in-house development capabilities through platforms like TRUBOX and Pressbooks allow us to support boutique projects and streamline creation using customizable templates.

Knowledge Makers/ UNSG Fellowship / A Study of the Value of Kamloops Parks
Kamloops Accessibility Map / Foodloops / BIOL 1592

Fall 2025 and Beyond

  • PIDP
  • Moodle (new upgrade features & design practices)
  • Digital Literacy Challenge
  • AI Workshops (TBD)
  • GenAI Quickstart
  • AI Fluency for Educators Course
  • Intro to Blended Learning
  • Other ideas?

Contact us:

Director of LT&I: Brian Lamb blamb@tru.ca

Support team:
Coordinators, Educational Technologies: Jamie Drozda, Melanie Latham, Brad Forsyth, Brenna Clarke Gray (on leave)
Learning Technologists: Stephanie Gountas, Jeisil Aguilar, Alexandra Floyd
Video Producer: Jon Fulton

Email:
moodlesupport@tru.ca and/or learningtech@tru.ca

item.title: WordPress for Student Portfolios
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: WordPress is one of the world’s most popular platforms for publishing and sharing content on the web, powering approximately 30% of all websites. Among its many possible uses in education, WordPress has proven especially useful in allowing students to share examples of their academic and professional work creatively and in ways which can add significantly to their learning in courses and programs of. TRU hosts a local instance of WordPress through its TRUBox sites which means that students can create engaging presentations of their academic work in ways which are compliant with Canadian and provincial privacy legislation (such as FIPPA). In this interactive workshop we will explore and discuss examples of student portfolios at TRU. You will have the opportunity to register for a TRUBox account; create a portfolio assignment using WordPress; and become familiar with support for WordPress-based assignments by working with TRU faculty and staff.
item.excerpt:encoded: WordPress has been successfully used by hundreds of students at TRU to build customized online portfolios. Come see what's possible!

item.title: Learning Technology Community of Practice
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: Come meet to discuss your learning technology project! Share experiences and insights with likeminded faculty and staff. Plan your project or discover ideas for a project.
item.excerpt:encoded: Share experiences and insights with like-minded faculty and staff. Plan your project or discover ideas for a project.

item.title: (Web) Literacy Across the Curriculum
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: Canadian philosopher Marshall McLuhan famously stated “The medium is the message” (Understanding Media, 1964). More than fifty years later, this statement resonates more strongly than ever— particularly in the “online era”. In this discussion-focused workshop we will explore how learning outcomes in course syllabi which reference media and technology, and how the kinds of technology used to teach courses, can affect students’ learning. Participants should bring a syllabus from a course they currently teach (or plan to teach) to think about, annotate, discuss— and possibly redesign— as per McLuhan’s statement.
item.excerpt:encoded: In this workshop we'll discuss how the kinds of technology we use to teach courses can affect students’ learning.

item.title: An Introduction to Blended Learning
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: “Blended Learning” is a term that is widely (and colloquially) used when discussing teaching and learning in face-to-face settings with the assistance of online technologies. But what does this mean? In their widely-cited Blended Learning in Higher Education (2008), Garrison and Vaughan describe blended learning as “the thoughtful fusion of face-to-face and online learning experiences” (p.5). In this discussion-based workshop we will highlight and explore salient points from Garrison and Vaughn’s text; discuss their Community of Inquiry (CoI) model which can help inform blended approaches to teaching and learning; and brainstorm how blended approaches might be helpful in participants’ specific teaching situations.
item.excerpt:encoded: What is it? And how can it inform course and program development?

item.title: Team Communication with Mattermost
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: In this session we will explore features, functionality, and user experience of Mattermost, a free chat and collaboration tool hosted at TRU. An increasingly popular application for team-based projects, Mattermost will be valuable for teachers, students, or anyone who is involved in distributed teamwork for projects of any scale. As it is hosted at TRU, it is compliant with privacy legislation (FIPPA). Participants will have the opportunity to initiate an instance of Mattermost; populate this with files and links; create channels; and invite additional users— including colleagues outside of TRU. TRU use cases will explored so participants can see how Mattermost might fit in with their projects or course delivery.
item.excerpt:encoded: Mattermost is an open-source communication platform which allows for rapid and flexible collaboration. It's especially powerful for distributed teams.

item.title: Learning Analytics: Affordances and Cautions
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: The term “Learning Analytics” refers to “the measurement, collection, analysis and reporting of data about learners and their contexts, for purposes of understanding and optimising learning and the environments in which it occurs” (Siemens, 2010). In this discussion-focused workshop we will explore this definition more closely; identify sources of learning analytics in Moodle and other online learning applications; brainstorm how analytics can be used in specific teaching situations, and discuss why it is important to be cautious when using analytics, particularly with respect to student privacy.
item.excerpt:encoded: We'll identify sources of learning analytics in Moodle and other applications, brainstorm how analytics can be used, and discuss why it is important to be cautious when using analytics, particularly with respect to student privacy.

item.title: Live from Anywhere: Web Conferencing with Big Blue Button
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: Big Blue Button (BBB) is a web-based conferencing system which includes audio, video, slides, chat, and screen sharing capability. At TRU we host our own instance of BBB, which means that it is compliant with federal and provincial privacy legislation. It is available for use within Moodle, and through Mattermost. Through Mattermost, BBB can be used to connect with colleagues outside TRU. BBB sessions can also be recorded and shared for later use. In this session, participants will learn more about the features and functionality of BBB; initiate, record, and share a Big Blue Button video conferencing session in Moodle or Mattermost; and design a lesson plan for a class that includes the use of BBB.
item.excerpt:encoded: BBB allows for live classroom and web conferencing. It can be launched from Moodle, Mattermost, or as a standalone tool for webinars.

item.title: Ed Tech and the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL)
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: With the increased use of online technologies teaching and learning in higher education, so too has there been an increase in the number of peer-reviewed journals which publish articles on how technology is being used in a wide range of academic subject areas and settings. This kind of teacher-lead research is often referred to as the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL). SoTL studies, discussion papers, and other kinds of scholarly writing focusing on have appeared in The International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning (IRRODL); The Canadian Journal for the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (CJSoTL); Tech Trends; and elsewhere. In this discussion-focused workshop we will identify and describe some of the leading publications which deal with learning technology and SoTL, and brainstorm ideas for educational technology-focused studies, and discuss how these could be designed, implemented, and published.
item.excerpt:encoded: We will identify and describe some of the leading publications which deal with learning technology and SoTL, and brainstorm ideas for educational technology-focused studies.

item.title: The ABC’s of Universal Design for Learning
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: Universal Design for Learning (UDL) is a research-informed framework that can be used to guide the design of learning environments to remove barriers to accessibility for all learners. In this session we will explore concepts and principles associated with UDL and discuss how these relate to participants’ specific teaching situations. Participants will have the opportunity to review their syllabi, slides, handouts, and other materials and redesign these as per good Universal Design for Learning (UDL) practice.
item.excerpt:encoded: We will explore concepts and principles associated with UDL and discuss how these relate to participants’ specific teaching situations.

item.title: Educational Radio: Podcasting for Teaching and Learning
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: Podcasting is now mainstream to the point that it has entered the Oxford English Dictionary: “A digital audio file of speech, music, broadcast material, etc., made available on the internet for downloading to a computer or portable media player; a series of such files, new instalments of which can be received by subscribers automatically”. TRU’s Centre for Excellence in Learning and Teaching (CELT) hosts an ongoing series of educational podcasts, among dozens of others focused on teaching and learning. Podcasting can provide students and instructors the opportunity to reach a potentially wide audience of listeners and share persistent, immediate audio records of discussions, interviews, and other kinds of content. In this interactive workshop we will explore the “educational podcast” landscape; learn steps involved in recording and sharing audio for a podcast; as well as exploring websites and software commonly associated with podcasting.
item.excerpt:encoded: We'll go over how to record, edit, and share digital audio for your course and beyond.

item.title: Lightboards 101
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded:
Hi, I’m Jon Fulton and I work as a video producer for Open Learning here at TRU. Over the years I have worked with instructional designers, instructors and course developers to create a variety of media products for distance learning.  From talking head video, classroom lecture capture, voice over powerpoint, onlocation, greenscreen or interviews. Recently I have started to work with a device called a lightboard. The lightboard was first developed at Northwestern University and they have a terrific webpage which outlines how to build one and some best practices.

Here is the URL:

https://lightboard.info

A Lightboard is basically a transparent whiteboard like in a classroom that you record on video while looking into the camera.  The instructor can write on the board in real time or super impose images without turning away from the viewer. This is the key that makes the light board exciting for me; it allows the instructor to maintain eye contact with the audience or student while lecturing, which I believe helps with engagement.

Here are some examples of what it looks like.

Here is how I made mine.

Here is how others have made theirs.

In our workshop I will let you play with the DIY Lightboard I have built and talk about best practices and other tips and tricks.
item.excerpt:encoded: Lightboards allow you produce a video while writing or drawing on a board of illuminated glass in front of you. Let's make some explainers!

item.title: Creating and Curating Educational Playlists With LinkedIn Learning
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: TRU faculty, students, and staff now have access to 5300+ online courses through LinkedIn Learning (TRU IT Services). LinkedIn Learning (formerly Lynda.com) is a subsidiary of web-based business service platform LinkedIn (acquired by Microsoft in 2016). In this session we will explore the features and functionality of TRU’s instance of the LinkedIn Learning platform; learn how to create and share playlists of videos and other content; and discuss how this might be used in participants’ specific teaching and learning situations.
item.excerpt:encoded: TRU faculty, students, and staff now have access to 5300+ online courses through LinkedIn Learning (formerly Lynda.com).

item.title: A Survey of Open Texts and OER Repositories
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: BC— through BCCampus, and through collaborations involving faculty, staff and students— is leading the way in the creation and sharing of open textbooks and open educational resources (OERs). Many open texts can be found through the BCCampus website; but there are others. In this discussion-focused workshop we will explore Open Educational Resource (OER) repositories and identify curricular materials available through these in various subject areas which may be suitable for participants’ teaching situations. We will also explore grants, fellowships, and other opportunities through BCCampus, TRU, and other institutions and agencies which provide opportunities and support for faculty and staff who wish to create an Open Text or otherwise use OER.
item.excerpt:encoded: We will explore Open Educational Resource (OER) repositories and identify curricular materials that are free to use and to adapt.

item.title: Publishing and Adapting Content with Pressbooks
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: Pressbooks is a platform for creating open textbooks which can then be shared and, if you choose, adapted by others. In this session we will discuss the benefits associated with open texts for faculty and students; create a Pressbooks account; learn the steps to create a Pressbooks open text; we will also discuss support available at TRU for those interested in getting started with Pressbooks.
item.excerpt:encoded: Pressbooks is a WordPress-based platform focused on print and electronic book creation. It's BC's preferred system for creating and customizing open textbooks.

item.title: Connectivism and Connectivist Approaches to Teaching and Learning
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: Since 2005, connectivism has been the subject of a wide range of articles, blog posts, courses, and other kinds of media and learning experiences. Connectivism is a theory of learning that places emphasis on connections between and among networks of learners (Siemens, 2005). It has been described as its own generation of distance education pedagogy (Anderson and Dron, 2011) and a “learning theory for the digital age” (Siemens, 2005). Controversially, Siemens has stated that as per this theory, knowledge may reside in “non-human appliances”. In this discussion-focused session we will explore concepts and assumptions associated with connectivist pedagogy; determine if connectivism is as relevant in 2019 as it was in 2005; and brainstorm how connectivist approaches might be used to enhance teaching and learning in specific subject areas.
item.excerpt:encoded: Connectivism is a widely cited and controversial theory of teaching and learning "for the digital age". How can it be used in your course or teaching situation?

item.title: Learning to SPLOT
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded: SPLOT stands for “Smallest Possible Learning Online Tools”. These are WordPress-based tools for teaching and learning which do not require accounts or logins for users. Available free to any educator in BC higher ed through the Open Ed Tech Coop, SPLOT applications include the SPLOT-Writer (primarily for writing and publishing); the SPLOT-Collector (for collections of images); and SPLOT-Box (for audio and video content). In this session participants will explore existing SPLOTs from TRU and elsewhere; explore features and functionality of SPLOTs; brainstorm how SPLOTs could be used for their specific course or project; and learn about what supports are available at TRU and through the Open ETC for those who wish to use SPLOTs or learn more.
item.excerpt:encoded: SPLOTs strip down online publishing to its most basic form, and respect privacy by not requiring accounts or logins for authoring.

item.title: Productivity & Creativity in the Cloud with Microsoft Office 365
item.dc:creator: mstranach
item.content:encoded:
Session Description

TRU faculty, students, and staff now have free access to Office 365. This includes access to a wide range of Microsoft apps. Some of these--- like Word, Excel, and PowerPoint--- will likely be familiar. Others--- like Forms, Stream, Sway, and Kaizala--- will be possibly new. In this session we will explore the full extent of TRU's 365 offering; learn how to create and share content using one or more of the 365 apps; and discuss how 365 apps might be used in participants’ specific teaching and learning situations.

Session Agenda

  • Let's register for TRU's 365 offering!
  • What does this include?
    • What are some of these?
    • How do we use these?
  • Let's create some content using a 365 app!
  • Let's share some content with colleagues or students!
  • Can you see using these apps in your class? What about in other situations?

Facilitated By:

Matt Stranach

Coordinator, Educational Technologies

Please email mstranach@tru.ca to share your work or with further questions.

Try It Yourself!

This short video will show you the steps you need to follow in order to gain access to TRU's Office 365 offering; it will also show you some of the apps which are included.

We will spend time during the workshop focussing on the 365 apps that you are interested in!

Can't make it to the Kamloops campus? This workshop is also available through web conferencing. Please email Matt if you are interested in this option.

Further Resources

  • TRU ITS page for student access to Office 365
  • TRU ITS page for faculty and staff access to Office 365 (staff intranet)
  • TRU privacy notification for Office 365
  • LinkedIn Learning video playlist on Office 365 for the classroom (sign-in required)

If you missed this session, share your contact information with us and we'll be in touch for the next offering of this workshop.
item.excerpt:encoded: TRU faculty, students, and staff now have free access to Office 365. Learn how to create and share content using 365 apps, and explore how 365 apps might be used in your specific teaching situation.

item.title: Accessibility with Texthelp Read&Write
item.dc:creator: mstranach
item.content:encoded:
Session Description

TRU faculty, students, and staff now have access to Texthelp Read&Write. Read&Write has a wide range of features which can help make online teaching materials more accessible including:

  • text to speech,
  • dictionary,
  • picture dictionary,
  • prediction work suggestions,
  • highlighters,
  • personal vocabulary glossary,
  • a "check it" function for spelling, grammar and word errors

In this session we will explore the features and functionality of TRU’s instance of Read&Write; render course content using specific features; and discuss how Read&Write might be used in participants’ specific teaching and learning situations.

Session Agenda

  • Let’s register for TRU’s Read&Write offering!
  • How does this work?
  • Let's explore some of these cool features!
    • Text to speech, picture dictionary, highlighters, others
  • But how does it work with Moodle?
  • Let’s render some of our own content content using the Read&Write features of our choosing!
  • Let’s share and discuss the Read&Write renderings of our content!
  • Can you see using this program yourself?
  • Do you think this would be helpful for your students?

Facilitated By:

Matt Stranach

Coordinator, Educational Technologies

Please email mstranach@tru.ca to share your work or with further questions.

Try It Yourself!

This short video will show you the steps you need to follow in order to gain access to TRU’s instance of Read&Write.

We will spend time during the workshop focussing on the Read&Write features that you are interested in!

Can’t make it to the Kamloops campus? This workshop is also available through web conferencing. Please email Matt if you are interested in this option.

Further Resources

  • TRU ITS page for access to Read&Write

item.title: Cloud Computing
item.dc:creator: troy
item.content:encoded:
“…it's cloud's illusions I recall…”[ref]http://jonimitchell.com/music/song.cfm?id=83[/ref]

[dropcap]T[/dropcap]he "Cloud" has become a staple of everyday computing. We can store our documents in the cloud, create content in the cloud and use a variety of cloud applications. We can move from work to home to the beach and there's our stuff, conveniently located in the cloud. There are a variety of different types of cloud providers each promising improvement and convenience in our lives in some way. But what are these cloud services really, and is there a downside?

What is the cloud?

The very phrase "the cloud" conjures up something fluffy, ephemeral, mutable and in flux. Some definitions gathered from the the internet give us:
In cloud computing, the word cloud (also phrased as "the cloud") is used as a metaphor for "the Internet," so the phrase cloud computing means "a type of Internet-based computing," where different services — such as servers, storage and applications — are delivered to an organization's computers and devices through the Internet. [ref]http://www.webopedia.com/TERM/C/cloud_computing.html[/ref]
Or perhaps a bit more to the point:
“Cloud” is a buzzword that vaguely suggests the promise and convenience of being able to access files from anywhere. But the reality is that the cloud is hardly floating like mist above our heads — it’s a physical infrastructure, it's many computers housed in massive warehouses all over the world. And yet as long as it’s easy to read email on our phones and watch movies on our laptops, we generally don’t take the time to wonder where our data actually goes, how it gets there, and what happens to it on its way.[ref]http://gizmodo.com/what-is-the-cloud-and-where-is-it-1682276210[/ref]
I like to paraphrase it this way:
The cloud is somebody else's computer.

The upside

The cloud provides us with many wonderful capabilities from basic file storage to full blown applications that provide us with useful functionality. As identified in the first definition above "the cloud" is just a euphemism for "the internet". So basically anything you do over the internet is in "the cloud". There is a staggering array of modern computing conveniences that fall into this category: social spaces such as Facebook, Twitter and Instagram; file storage facilities such as onedrive, dropbox, google docs; and full blown application environments such as google apps, evernote, and office live. There are advantages afforded by cloud computing:
  • the functionality and computing power that runs these things is taken care of by someone else;
  • your stuff is often easy to distribute to other people and may also include the ability to collaborate;
  • you can move across the different devices in your life and get at all of your stuff;
  • you don't need to do as much installing of software, filing your computer files and that sort of thing.

The downside

To fully understand the downsides of the cloud, let's refer back to my version of the definition "the cloud is somebody else's computer." Further, let's draw an analogy. Let's say you are spending a week at my place and decide that keeping your supply of wine in my wine fridge affords you many conveniences, it is close at hand and because my wine fridge is cold your wine will also be cold when you want to use it. There are also some risks involved though, I might not recognize it as your wine, after all I also have wine in the fridge. I might believe as a matter of operating principle that any wine in my wine fridge is mine to use as I see fit, in essence I see the ownership of the wine transferring to me once you close the fridge door. Enough of the silly analogy, it begins to break down pretty quickly. In general though, when you put something in the cloud you are surrendering a great deal of control of whatever you have put there. This can extend to a number of issues: ownership, usage, privacy, etc. Most cloud providers have a set of terms/privacy policy that outline how your stuff will be used. These terms may also change from time to time so it is important to keep up on them. Remember that these policies don't protect you and your stuff from hackers who break into those cloud providers. Another issue that is continually played out in the courts concerns legal jurisdictions and what laws will preside in event of an issue. For most Canadians, especially those involved in education, government or other areas where federal and provincial privacy legislation applies, cloud computing is particularly problematic. As an example, the US Homeland Security act means that stuff stored on computers in the United States cannot satisfy Canadian privacy legislation. Further, lots of cloud providers have multiple servers in multiple geographic locations.

The danger

There are also many risks to putting your stuff on "somebody" else's computer. For instance, they might decide to use it for some purpose that you are not necessarily comfortable with. There is a saying that if you aren't paying for a product, then you are the product. Services such as Facebook are fond of conducting research using the data on their servers. In the academic world we are familiar with research ethics application and approval processes. Such things are mostly absent in the cloud. What about informed consent? Sadly, we have consented. Surely you remember reading the account agreement when you signed up. It's my personal belief that we have yet to see what I call Zuckerberg's punchline. I'm not sure what form it will take, but after decades of us happily posting the details of our carefully curated lives, our interests, our photos, our families, our ideologies and beliefs; and after those same decades of research into human nature, consumer preferences, potential danger to the realm, the whole package gets bundle up and sold to the highest bidder.

What to do, what to do

I have a small set of guidelines I use with respect to cloud computing:
  1. if you want to retain control over ownership and usage be very careful about putting it in the cloud. If you do make sure you understand the termsof the provider.
  2. If privacy legislation is an issue follow the advice of your company or organization with respect to approved cloud services.
  3. If personal privacy is an issue then don't put it on the internet. Anywhere. If you take photographs with your mobile make sure that it does not automatically upload them somewhere for your convenience.
  4. The question to ask is will this document, tweet, photograph, etc. cause me some concern if it were shared with everyone on the planet. If it will, don't put it in the internet.
  5. If I wouldn't toss it on a table at Starbucks then walk away from it, I won't store it in the cloud.

 An exit strategy

Probably the most important thing to have is an exist strategy. There are many well known and lesser known closures of cloud services that have left users scrambling to retrieve their stuff or make other arrangements to replace the lost functionality. The closure of Google's Reader rss service pretty much relegated the world of rss to a niche sub-culture and almost killed it. I became almost suicidal when an email/project management/productivity service called IQTELL announced it would close about a year ago. (Luckily their community rallied and the company worked hard to maintain their service.) I had used this on a daily basis and continue to, it is simply the best thing I've discovered for organizing my life. Always in the back of your mind should be the question, what if this service closes. Will I lose anything, how can I retrieve my stuff? Okay, time to wrap this rambling screed.

“I've looked at clouds from both sides now From up and down, and still somehow It's cloud illusions I recall I really don't know clouds at all” [ref]http://jonimitchell.com/music/song.cfm?id=83[/ref]

item.title: Tool Write Up Template
item.dc:creator: troy
item.content:encoded:
Instructions: delete when finished

  • Do Not author in the template post. Use the "Copy All Content" command on the "vertical ellipsis below your avatar and above the sidebar. Then go to the existing posts I set up during our proof of concept work (or a new post if no post exists for the tool you are writing about) and paste at the bottom. Existing draft work will still be in place for copy and pasting.
  • If you need to make changes to this template, use Save Draft when done, rather than publish.
  • Set a feature image in sidebar->document tab->Feature Image. Note you can use the instant images sidebar (tab that looks like a lightening blot) to search and download images from unsplash. Although some other image, such as a screen shot, may be more appropriate.
  • Set the correct parent (eg Tools) and subcategory (eg TRU Tools in the sidebar->document tab->Categories and turn off the template category.
  • Add any tags that you wish.
  • Add a short excerpt (document tab in right sidebar), a sentence or two at most, that introduces this tool on the catalog page.
  • Areas of this page use the Info box block from the Ultimate Addons category. In most cases you will be fine with this blocks, although on occasion you may need to add additional blocks of other kinds as required (e.g. embed blocks in the TRU Faculty section).
  • For the "This tool is good for" section, reveal tool features via use cases
  • The "other notes and questions" section is meant to provide a few useful snippets or answers to common questions. Each item should have a title and be closed by default. There are only two right now, but you can duplicate the block as needed.

item.title: Workshop Template
item.dc:creator: troy
item.content:encoded:
Instructions: delete when finished

  • Do Not author in the template post. Use the "Copy" link for the template entry in the All Posts list. Change the title of the post right away and Save Draft.
  • If you need to make changes to this template, use Save Draft when done, rather than publish.
  • Set a feature image in sidebar->document tab->Feature Image. Note you can use the instant images sidebar (tab that looks like a lightening blot) to search and download images from unsplash. Although some other image may be more appropriate.
  • Set the correct parent (eg Workshops) and subcategory (eg Moodle in the sidebar->document tab->Categories and turn off the template category.
  • Add any tags that you wish.
  • Add a short excerpt (document tab in right sidebar), a sentence or two at most, that introduces this Workshop on the listing page.
  • An info box block has been included in this template, but it may not be necessary to use it. Add other blocks such as heading, list, expand/more blocks as required.

This is the workshop description. Add other formatting blocks: subheads, list blocks as necessary. An info text block is below.

Heading

Click here to change this text. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit. Ut elit tellus, luctus nec ullamcorper mattis, pulvinar dapibus leo.

item.dc:creator: bgray
item.content:encoded:
Session Description

Warheads barbie shania twain vanilla coke minesweeper, baby got back I will be your father figure bleached hair jeans lion king. Toyota supra I will always love you rachel green alternative rock nickelodeon velcro sneakers. Toy story choker necklace speed sup frosted tips. I don’t want no scrubs napster west wing boombox. Street fighter ii koosh ball uncle phil titanic, mtv inflatable furniture sports utility vehicles scrolling text doug ford explorer.

[LibCal Registration Button Here]

What You Can Expect

  • Good will hunting bubble tape butterfly clips independence day, skifree world wide web speed harrison ford hey arnold paper fortune teller.
  • Koosh ball royal stewart tartan toni braxton keds g-shocks wallet chains, buddy list oakleys men in black digital pets.
  • Beavis and butthead chia pet baby got back nerf guns vcr cargo pants.
  • Tom hanks vanilla ice schindler’s list pokémon carpenter pants

Interested in this topic but missed this workshop? We'll let you know next time we're offering a session.

item.title: Create Share and Reuse Interactive Content - Part 1 (Moodle)
item.dc:creator: jdrozda
item.content:encoded:
Session Description

This is the first of a three part series on creating interactive content; we encourage you to attend all three. By the end of this workshop you will have experience creating an interactive video in Moodle; you may even walk away with an interactive video to share with your students and peers! We will be using the H5P activity in Moodle to make an HTML5-based interactive video which allows you to add multiple choice and fill in the blank questions, pop-up text and other types of interactions.

Session Agenda

  • Presentation of H5P's interactive video content type.
  • Walk through of adding the activity type in Moodle.
  • Guided overview of adding multiple choice and fill in the blank questions as well as pop-up text to your video.
  • Time to play and ask questions!

Facilitated By:

Jamie Drozda
and
Brenna Clarke Gray

Please email jdrozda@tru.ca or bgray@tru.ca to share your work or with further questions.

Try It Yourself!

One way to get started is by reusing an H5P content type. Download the example interactive video by clicking on Reuse link in the bottom left corner of the content. Now you can upload this file to your Moodle course by clicking Add an activity or resource and selecting Interactive Content for the activity list.

Next, click the "Upload" tab at the top to upload an existing .h5p file. Select a file to upload and click "Use". The editor will now load and you can start editing H5P content. Here you may edit all fields in the H5P. Saving will update the H5P as well. Use "Tutorial" and "Example" links at the top to learn more about this content type and to see some examples of usage.

Another way to get started is to create a new interactive video in Moodle. In your Moodle course click Add an activity or resource and select Interactive Content. Type "Interactive video" in the Search content types text area, click Details then Use. Here you may edit all fields in the H5P. Saving will update the H5P as well. Use "Tutorial" and "Example" links at the top to learn more about this content type and to see some examples of usage.

[h5p id="5"]

Further Resources

Some other resources you may find helpful:

  • If you’d like to review the functions we’ve talked about today, like uploading, authoring, and downloading, the basic H5P Content Author Guide offers easy-to-follow directions with screenshots.
  • H5P also provides thorough tutorials for each of the content types they offer.
  • Pressbooks provides more information about its integration with H5P in its User Guide.
  • More information about integrating your H5P interactives into your Moodle course space is provided in Moodle’s documentation.

If you missed this session, share your contact information with us and we'll be in touch for the next offering of this workshop.

item.title: Creating and Curating Educational Playlists With LinkedIn Learning
item.dc:creator: mstranach
item.content:encoded:
Session Description

TRU faculty, students, and staff now have access to 5300+ online courses through LinkedIn Learning. LinkedIn Learning is a subsidiary of web-based business service platform LinkedIn. In this session we will explore the features and functionality of TRU’s instance of the LinkedIn Learning platform; learn how to create and share playlists of videos and other content; and discuss how these might be used in participants’ specific teaching and learning situations.

Session Agenda

  • Let’s log in to LinkedIn Learning through TRU!
  • What exactly is this?
  • Why would I want to use this?
  • What kind of content is there and how could it be helpful?
  • Let’s find some relevant videos!
  • Let’s compile these videos into a playlist!
  • Let's share playlists with colleagues and/or students!
  • Let's modify our playlists!
  • Do you think these videos would be helpful for your students?
  • Do you think it would be helpful for your students to create and share their own playlists?

Facilitated By:

Matt Stranach

Coordinator, Educational Technologies

Please email mstranach@tru.ca to share your work or with further questions.

Try It Yourself!

This short video will show you the steps you need to follow in order to gain access to LinkedIn Learning through TRU.

item.title: Meme Media: Making and Using Attention-Grabbing Images and Animated GIFs
item.dc:creator: blamb
item.content:encoded:
Session Description

The meme: the direct, often wild small piece of media that can pop up in the strangest ways and in the strangest places.

In this session we will focus on the practical elements of making memes and animated GIFs. We'll walk through a few tools and techniques that will have you sharing your inspirations with your friends, your students and your social media networks.

While we build, we will also talk a little bit about the social dimension of this form of media. We'll discuss how memes are playing an arguably out-sized influence on our contemporary discourse, and also consider a few ways memes can go wrong.

Session Agenda

  • Let's share a favourite meme!
  • A short history of the meme.
  • Make a meme in less than five minutes!
  • Making animated GIFs from images or videos. How are GIFs used for instruction? Let's see if we can make an "explainer GIF".
  • While we work, let's talk about how memes are deployed in online culture... While fun, memes have been weaponized for propaganda and can perpetuate harmful representation.
  • What can we do if we want to go deeper or be more advanced?

Facilitated By:

Brenna Clarke Gray & Brian Lamb

Try It Yourself!

This short screencast tries to demonstrate one technique from this workshop: how to pull a looping clip from an online video. This particular demo uses the Giphy GIF Maker. This tool is not the most precise option, but it's easy to learn and lots of fun.

It would be nice if Brian could stop going on about vintage synthesizers. But you gotta admit this introduction to the Mellotron from British Pathé is pretty sweet.

Further Resources

  • r/educationalgifs. A frequently updated collection of GIFs that illustrate principles or generally show amazing things.
  • Common Craft, "How to Make Explainer GIFs". If you are a confident PowerPoint user, you might find these techniques especially useful.
  • Stephanie (Charlie) Farley, University of Edinburgh, Gif It Up – Create your own Gifs. "This workshop was created to provide an introduction to creating GIFs from openly licensed and public domain, museum, library, and archival materials. Using free and open online tools."
  • Michael Branson Smith, "A History of the GIF". A collection of links, with many early and influential examples.
  • Know Your Meme. A "site that researches and documents Internet memes and viral phenomena."
  • Erinn Wong, "Digital Blackface: How 21st Century Internet Language Reinforces Racism"

If you missed this session, share your contact information with us and we'll be in touch for the next offering of this workshop.

item.title: Is Anybody Out There?: Tech Tools for Feedback
item.dc:creator: bgray
item.content:encoded:
Session Description

It's the age-old question: Do your students read your feedback? And when you're in the classroom, do you know when your materials have landed with students? Feedback is difficult, and making it meaningful is even more so. In this session, we'll look at three tools for making feedback more efficient, timely, and relevant to students and engaging for everyone: animated gifs, polls, and video feedback for assignments. We'll practice using all three and discuss what situations might be best served by each method. By the end of the session, you'll be able to implement at least one new tool in your classes immediately.

Session Agenda

  • Discussion of current feedback strategies: what works, what doesn't, and in what contexts.
  • What problem did you come here to solve today?
  • Overview of the three strategies with time to play with each one:
    • Am I getting through?: Polls for Assessing Learning
    • What are they thinking?: Animated GIFS for Immediate Classroom Feedback
    • Meet them where they're at: Video Feedback on Assignments
  • The take-home: what is one strategy you tried today that you can implement this week?

Facilitated By:

Brenna Clarke Gray

Coordinator, Educational Technologies

Please email bgray@tru.ca to share your work or with further questions.

Try It Yourself!

We're going to spend some time in this workshop thinking about how students can use GIFs for feedback on their learning. For example, if students could submit one animated gif to replace your course description in the university calendar, what might they choose?

In 2014, I asked students to write their course evaluations in the form of GIFs. I made an example for them, and two responses still live online: here and here.

Think about your trickiest assignment: what might students choose if they could tell you how they felt in animated GIFs? Check out the video for more discussion of how to do this.

Further Resources

  • This video shows how polling is used in one Harvard graduate class to check understanding and stimulate discussion.
  • GIFs aren't just for the classroom -- they're the language of the internet. This article explains why, and argues that you should get fluent.
  • Some instructors are using video feedback to show students what the experience of reading their work looks like.
  • Researchers are proving that video feedback is more engaging, but the jury is still out about the impact on learning.

If you missed this session, share your contact information with us and we'll be in touch for the next offering of this workshop.
item.excerpt:encoded: This workshop will offer new tools for giving feedback to students in ways they may connect with more readily.

item.title: Knowledge Mobilization and You: Scholarly Podcasting for the Whole TRU Community
item.dc:creator: bgray
item.content:encoded:
Session Description

Podcasting is everywhere right now. Podcasts can reach huge and broad audiences, finding listeners with interest in scholarship regardless of their profession or education. Podcasts can also be a deeply intimate means of communicating information -- after all, most people listen to podcasts using headphones, in a one-on-one relationship (however one-sided). But podcasting is also a skill to develop that requires a particular set of tools. Is podcasting the right knowledge mobilization tool for your project? Is it useful in your classroom context? This session will help you decide, and get you started off on the right foot if the answer is yes.

Session Agenda

  • What makes podcasting so popular?
  • Examples of successful current incarnations of scholarly podcasts, broadly conceived.
  • Cultural conventions of podcasting.
  • Is your project a good fit for a podcast? What can podcasting look like within the classroom context?
  • The podcaster's toolkit:
    • The essential tools.
    • The essential skills.
    • Accessibility concerns.
    • The nice-to-haves.
    • Distribution and marketing.

Facilitated By:

Brenna Clarke Gray

Coordinator, Educational Technologies

Please email bgray@tru.ca to share your work or with further questions.

Try It Yourself!

Deciding whether your project is a good fit for podcasting is not easy. Reflect on the following key components to help make that decision:

  • Do you have time? Podcasting requires not just time to record, but to edit your audio to produce the best possible final product. Creating things like transcripts also takes time.
  • Is the project conversational? Can you chat about it, ideally with someone else?
  • Do you want public input? Many podcast listeners feel they have a certain amount of ownership of or engagement with a podcast, especially if they like it. Are you ready to engage meaningfully?

The videoblog gives you a little more context for thinking through these questions.

Further Resources

  • Some great podcasts you should check out if you're curious about the range of what scholars are doing with podcasting:
    • Secret Feminist Agenda, a SSHRC-funded podcast about contemporary feminist issues and on-the-ground feminist activism. Secret Feminist Agenda is peer-reviewed, and you can learn about how that works here.
    • Crackdown is a SSHRC- and CIHR-funded podcast about drugs and drug policy made by drug users and informed by research.
  • University Affairs did a thoughtful piece on the potential of podcasting for academics in 2017.
  • There are lots of good resources about making podcasts accessible, but this one is the easiest to read and adopt.
  • This article reckons that 2019 was the year of the podcast in academia (I'm less sure).

If you missed this session, share your contact information with us and we'll be in touch for the next offering of this workshop.
item.excerpt:encoded: This session will give an overview of what you need to be an effective podcaster, and also help you make decisions about whether podcasting is right for you.

item.title: Learning in the Open: Tools for Teaching on the Open Web
item.dc:creator: bgray
item.content:encoded:
Session Description

From more authentic assignments to more effective writing, there are a lot of great arguments for taking your teaching out of closed systems like Moodle and on to the open web. In this session, we will look at an introductory overview of three tools for teaching on the open web -- Wordpress, Wikipedia, and Twine -- and talk about the rewards (and risks!) of doing our learning and teaching in public. By the end of this session, you'll have had hands-on time with these tools and be able to decide if this kind of teaching is right for you.

Session Agenda

  • What do we mean by the "open web," and what are other educators doing with this space?
  • The benefits of open approaches to teaching and learning.
  • Risks and cautions for the use of open web tools.
  • Examples of and hands-on time with our featured tools:
    • Wordpress
    • Wikipedia
    • Twine
  • Next steps: how to pursue teaching with one of these tools.

Facilitated By:

Brenna Clarke Gray

Coordinator, Educational Technologies

Please email bgray@tru.ca to share your work or with further questions.

Try It Yourself!

In this screencast, you can check out what gameplay looks like for a Twine activity. This is a now-famous Twine game called Queers in Love at the End of the World, and has been seen as a transformative example of what Twine can do. It is also often used as an example of Twine for social justice education and empathy building. Once you've watched the screencast, try it out yourself and read a poem / article that suggests the power of this particular Twine activity.

Please note that Queers in Love at the End of the World is intended for adult learners and contains difficult situations and language that some users may find offensive.

  • Queers in Love at the End of the World
  • A poem the game inspired, published in The Guardian.

You can think of a Twine game as akin to a branching scenario or decision tree. How might this tool work for your teaching? Could students work through -- or even design themselves -- a relevant case study from your discipline, for example?

Further Resources

  • The teaching and learning folks at Vanderbilt University have built a nice guide for how and why you should encourage your students to blog.
  • And if you're thinking about blogging for your own work, Times Higher Education has an article about why you should.
  • Wiki Education wants to encourage you to teach with Wikipedia, and they will act as a bridge to help you build your assignments.
  • Wikipedia also keeps a list of school and university projects, which can provide great inspiration for your own teaching.
  • The Digital Writing and Research Lab at the University of Texas provides a lesson plan for using Twine in a writing class.
  • University of Illinois provides a thoughtful review of Twine.
  • Keegan Long-Wheeler offers three things he wished he knew before taking the plunge with Twine.

If you missed this session, share your contact information with us and we'll be in touch for the next offering of this workshop.
item.excerpt:encoded: Learn about how tools that live on the open web can change your teaching and the learning experiences for students.

item.title: Educational Technologies Community of Practice
item.dc:creator: bgray
item.content:encoded:
Session Description

What are the big questions you have about using educational technologies? What are the pedagogical implications of the choices we make? Where have your TRU colleagues found success -- or failure -- in playing with new ideas? In these relaxed, guided discussions, we'll dig into the big issues of EdTech and explore how to implement our theories in our practice.

What You Can Expect

Our Community of Practice sessions pick up where January's Digital Detox leaves off, giving you monthly opportunities to dig into the big issues of educational technologies and to strategize with your colleagues. Monthly meetings of the Educational Technologies Community of Practice are structured, community-led discussions, sometimes organized around readings or issues of importance to attendees. And the coffee is on us!

You can expect us to wrestle with some big issues, but also to spend a lot of time thinking about how to implement what we've learned. This is a great way to keep up your goals and changes in practice that you committed to in our Digital Detox.

Once you register, watch your email for updates about the monthly discussion topic -- and feel free to suggest something you're wrestling with.

If you missed this session, share your contact information with us and we'll be in touch for the next offering of this workshop.

item.title: Lightboards 101
item.dc:creator: bgray
item.content:encoded:
Session Description

In this session, led by Open Learning video producer Jon Fulton, participants will learn about different possibilities for using lightboards in the classroom (or for fun!). Jon will walk participants through how he built his lightboard, and everyone will have a chance to play with the lightboard while discussing best practices, tips, and tricks.

What You Can Expect

A lightboard is basically a transparent whiteboard (like in a classroom) that you record on video while looking into the camera. The instructor can write on the board in real time or super-impose images without turning away from the viewer. This is the key that makes the light board exciting: it allows the instructor to maintain eye contact with the audience or student while lecturing, which helps with engagement.

This technology was developed at Northwestern University, and you can read more about lightboards on their website.

If you missed this session, share your contact information with us and we'll be in touch for the next offering of this workshop.
item.excerpt:encoded: In this session, led by Open Learning video producer Jon Fulton, participants will learn about different possibilities for using lightboards in the classroom (or for fun!).

item.title: Digital Detox Coffee Chat
item.dc:creator: bgray
item.content:encoded:
Session Description

Over the course of our Digital Detox, we'll make time to get out from behind our computers and share a coffee while we discuss some of the big issues raised in the Digital Detox postings. To get the most out of these sessions, make sure you're registered in the TRU Digital Detox 2020: digitaldetox.trubox.ca.

What You Can Expect

Digital Detox Coffee Chats are facilitated discussions about key concepts from the Digital Detox postings, and will include ideas like:

  • EdTech and Equity Issues
  • Ethics and Data Privacy
  • Algorithms and Exclusion
  • Targeting of Students and Educators
  • Critical Digital Pedagogy
  • Radical Resistance
  • Radical Openness

We'll also work on setting goals for and changing behaviour in our own practice based on what we've learned.

If you missed this session, share your contact information with us and we'll be in touch for the next offering of this workshop.

item.dc:creator: bgray
item.content:encoded:
On September 9 and 10, scholars across Canada are participating in Scholar Strike Canada, in solidarity with the Scholar Strike happening in the US on September 8 and 9. Scholar Strike Canada, like its US counterpart, addresses systemic anti-Black violence and specifically anti-Blackness in the academy, and adds an additional focus on settler colonialism and anti-Indigeneity. More resources on Scholar Strike Canada, including an open letter in support that you can sign and teach-ins to attend virtually, are available here.

Educational technologies play a unique role in our current teaching climate, and they also -- like all aspects of academia -- have a history of policing Black and Indigenous bodies differently and more stringently than white bodies. Technologies are not neutral. For Scholar Strike Canada, I invite you to think about the technologies we use at TRU, and those we choose not to, from a perspective of equity and inclusion.

item.title: Trubox & Wordpress
item.dc:creator: troy
item.content:encoded:
Wordpress is currently used to power approximately 25% of all websites. Trubox is our general-use Wordpress installation, but we have others such as Pressbooks which is used for create open textbooks.

Use Wordpress when you want a teaching, learning or research-related website or blog. There are a variety of different uses live on trubox: class, faculty and student blogs; presentation and even support sites; sites that support various scholarly activity endeavours; and much more.
